response:
Reflection: the archive has converged on a robust core — industry-relative earnings yield paired with the deviation of the capex-to-gross-PPE rate from its own five-year norm (alpha 4.0–4.6%, t 3.5–4.1, Sharpe 0.5+). Three variants of that deviation (cardinal, volatility-standardized, industry-demeaned) all work at similar strength, so the mechanism is robust to normalization, and the persistence count works but is weaker, telling us magnitude beats a bounded regime indicator. Two clear negatives: spending *instability* (VOL) carries no alpha, so this is a first-moment expectation-error story, not a risk-of-erratic-management story; and adding a second discipline channel dilutes. Untested and high-value now: (i) whether the norm should exclude the current year, which currently contaminates the benchmark and mechanically shrinks the surprise; (ii) whether the alpha is concentrated in the overspending short leg, which the economic story predicts; (iii) whether the *valuation* leg can be strengthened (cyclically smoothed earnings, or a second cheapness channel), since every improvement so far came from the investment side; and (iv) whether the own-norm deviation functional form — the real discovery — transfers to working-capital and intangible/inorganic investment.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Cheap with capex above strictly past norm
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppegt), MA(LAG(RATIO(capx, ppegt), 1), 4))))
HYPOTHESIS: The benchmark for normal capital spending should be built only from prior years; including the current year in the moving average pulls the norm toward the observation being judged and understates genuine departures from established policy.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: This is a pure measurement repair of the current leader, isolating the single design choice of benchmark contamination while leaving the economics identical. If the surprise interpretation is correct, a lagged four-year norm should produce a larger, cleaner deviation and strengthen both the FMB slope and the FF5 alpha.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Cheap versus overspenders only
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(MUL(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppegt), MA(RATIO(capx, ppegt), 5)), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppegt), MA(RATIO(capx, ppegt), 5)), 0))))
HYPOTHESIS: The economic story is asymmetric: overvaluation of empire builders should be stronger and slower to correct than underappreciation of quiet retrenchers, so the discipline leg should only penalize spending above the firm's own norm and treat all below-norm spending as equally disciplined.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Half the current signal's dispersion comes from ranking degrees of underspending, which may be economically meaningless (a firm cutting 5% below norm is not twice as disciplined as one cutting 2.5%) and could be diluting the sort. Truncating at zero tests directly whether the alpha lives on the overinvestment short side, which would tell later generations where to concentrate.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Smoothed earnings yield with capex surprise
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(MA(ib, 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppegt), MA(RATIO(capx, ppegt), 5))))
HYPOTHESIS: Single-year earnings yield misclassifies cyclically depressed or temporarily inflated firms as cheap or expensive; a three-year average of income per dollar of market value measures durable price expectations, which is the right counterpart to a multi-year investment norm.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Every gain so far came from refining the investment leg while the valuation leg stayed a noisy one-year ratio, so the symmetric fix is to give both legs the same multi-year horizon. Smoothing should reduce the number of transient value traps entering the long leg and lower portfolio turnover without changing the economic channel.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Dual cheapness with capex restraint
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ppent, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), NEG(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppegt), MA(RATIO(capx, ppegt), 5))))
HYPOTHESIS: Earnings-based cheapness and replacement-cost cheapness are distinct price-expectation errors — one about profit persistence, one about asset value — and a firm cheap on both while spending below its own norm is the strongest disciplined-allocator candidate.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Both valuation legs independently generated roughly 4% alpha when paired with the same capex deviation, and unlike the two discipline legs (which diluted each other) they measure different objects, so their combination has a real chance of adding rather than substituting. This also keeps the valuation and investment halves equally weighted, so any improvement is attributable to the richer cheapness measure.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Cheap with inventory intensity at own norm
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5))))
HYPOTHESIS: Working-capital investment should be judged the same way as fixed investment: inventory held per dollar of sales rising above the firm's own established norm signals stock building on optimistic demand expectations, while a cheap firm operating at or below its normal inventory intensity is running a disciplined operation.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The genuine discovery in this archive is the own-norm deviation form, and the strongest earlier working-capital signal used a cruder growth-difference version of the same idea (alpha 2.9%); recasting it as an intensity deviation should sharpen it. It also tests whether the functional form is a general property of investment discipline rather than specific to physical capex.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Cheap without intangible asset buildup
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(SUB(RATIO(intan, at), MA(RATIO(intan, at), 5))))
HYPOTHESIS: Intangible assets on the balance sheet grow mainly through acquisitions and capitalized purchases, so an intangible share rising above the firm's own norm marks a firm buying growth and often overpaying, whereas cheap firms with stable intangible intensity are expanding, if at all, organically and within their means.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Raw acquisition flows failed twice (no alpha), but when acquisitions were folded into a capex own-norm deviation the signal worked (alpha 3.6%), suggesting the inorganic channel needs stock-based, self-benchmarked measurement rather than lumpy flow measurement. This is the cleanest untested version of that idea and is economically distinct from physical capacity spending.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
